subject: PDC CLO 1
description: Fundamentals of Big Data, distributed computing, HDFS architecture, CAP & ACID.

questions.text: A startup is collecting sensor readings from 50,000 IoT devices arriving every second, social-media stream data, and customer transaction logs all into a single analytics pipeline. The Chief Architect calls this a "Big Data problem." Which characteristic combination BEST justifies that label?
options: The data is stored only on a single RDBMS server with a fixed schema
The dataset is small but generated daily through ERP systems
High volume (TB/PB scale), high velocity (per-second), and variety (structured + semi-structured + unstructured)
The data has predictable arrival rate and is centrally managed
The data is purely transactional and requires immediate updates
questions.shortExplanation: Big Data is justified by huge Volume, fast Velocity, and mixed Variety together.
questions.explanation: A workload qualifies as Big Data when it shows three things at once: enormous size measured in terabytes or petabytes, very fast arrival speed such as per-second or millisecond streams, and a mix of data formats including structured tables, semi-structured logs, and unstructured text or media. A single traditional database server cannot keep up with all three at the same time, so a distributed platform is needed. These three together are commonly called the 3Vs of Big Data. The case described in the question shows all three signals, which is why the architect labels it a Big Data problem. The other options describe small, predictable, centrally managed, single-schema, or purely transactional systems, which are the opposite of a Big Data workload and do not need a distributed Big Data platform.

questions.text: A retail company's traditional CRM database is centrally managed, processes Gigabytes of structured transactions per day, and uses a strict schema. Compared to a typical Big Data system, what is the MOST significant architectural difference the team should expect when migrating?
options: Both systems require the same hardware configuration
Big Data system uses distributed storage with flat/dynamic schema instead of centralized strict-schema management
Big Data systems handle only structured data more efficiently
The CRM data is inherently more difficult to manage than Big Data
Both produce data with unknown relationships at the same frequency
questions.shortExplanation: Big Data uses distributed storage with a flexible schema instead of one strict central RDBMS.
questions.explanation: Traditional RDBMS systems keep all data on a single powerful server and force every record into a fixed schema set in advance. A Big Data platform like Hadoop spreads data across many low-cost machines and accepts data in flexible or dynamic formats, including JSON, logs, and images. This shift removes the single-server limit and lets the team grow storage and compute by adding more nodes. It also means planning for distributed file layouts, replication, and tools like Hive or Spark rather than pure SQL. The other options wrongly claim both systems need the same hardware, that Big Data only handles structured data, that RDBMS is harder to manage, or that velocities and patterns match, none of which reflect the real architectural shift.

questions.text: An e-commerce architect must decide how to scale a system that suddenly spikes from 10 TB/year to 10 PB/year. The traditional team suggests buying a bigger server with more RAM and CPU; the Big Data team proposes adding 100 commodity machines. Which scaling principle does each team represent?
options: Both teams propose horizontal scaling
Traditional team proposes horizontal scaling; Big Data team proposes vertical scaling
Traditional team proposes vertical scaling; Big Data team proposes horizontal scaling
Both teams propose vertical scaling
Neither team proposes a recognized scaling strategy
questions.shortExplanation: Vertical scaling means a bigger single machine; horizontal scaling means more machines.
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling, also called scaling up, upgrades a single server with more RAM, more CPU, or faster disks. Horizontal scaling, also called scaling out, adds more commodity machines into a cluster and shares the work across them. Vertical scaling is simple but hits a hardware ceiling and costs a lot at the top end. Horizontal scaling is the Big Data approach because it grows almost linearly with petabyte-scale data and tolerates node failures. The wrong options swap the two strategies, claim both teams use the same one, or deny that either is a real scaling strategy, all of which contradict the standard definitions taught in distributed computing.

questions.text: A media-analytics company uses a Hadoop cluster of 500 machines. The marketing manager asks, "Why does this cluster qualify as a 'distributed system' and not just a parallel processor on one big machine?" Which statement BEST captures the distinction?
options: The 500 nodes act as a single logical machine to clients while being physically interconnected; failure of one node doesn't crash the whole service
All 500 nodes share the same RAM and CPU bus
There is only one node performing all computation
The system cannot tolerate the failure of any single node
Parallel processing and distributed processing are exactly the same thing
questions.shortExplanation: A distributed system is many networked nodes that look like one service and survive node failures.
questions.explanation: A parallel computer is a single machine that uses many CPUs sharing the same memory and bus. A distributed system is many separate machines connected by a network. To the client they appear as one single logical service, but each node runs on its own. If one node crashes, the others keep serving requests, so the whole service does not go down. This network-based design is what makes Hadoop, Spark, and Kafka clusters truly distributed rather than just parallel. The other options confuse parallel and distributed, claim all nodes share one memory bus, say only one node computes, or wrongly state that one failure crashes the cluster, none of which match a real distributed architecture.

questions.text: A logistics firm chooses a distributed computing platform for fleet analytics. Their CTO lists three main benefits to the board. Which set correctly describes the MAIN benefits of distributed computing as taught in the course?
options: Performance, Scalability, Fault Tolerance
Centralization, Strict Schema, Single Point of Failure
Vertical Scaling, Single Node, Manual Recovery
RDBMS dependency, Schema rigidity, Low concurrency
ACID guarantees, Centralized storage, Synchronous replication only
questions.shortExplanation: The three main benefits are Performance, Scalability, and Fault Tolerance.
questions.explanation: Distributed computing wins on three points compared to a single server. Performance improves because tasks run in parallel on many nodes at once. Scalability improves because more machines can be added when data grows, without rewriting the system. Fault Tolerance improves because replication and failover let the cluster keep working even when individual nodes die. These three benefits together are the reason companies move from a single RDBMS to a Hadoop or Spark cluster. The other options list weaknesses such as vendor lock-in, single point of failure, vertical-only scaling, or manual failover, which are problems of centralized systems and not benefits of distributed ones.

questions.text: A Hadoop cluster has a single NameNode storing all file metadata, hierarchy, ACLs, and block map in RAM. The DevOps lead is asked to identify the single most critical risk of this design. What is it?
options: DataNodes will lose their data if NameNode reboots
NameNode is a single point of failure — if it fails, the entire HDFS becomes inaccessible
The cluster will automatically split-brain into two halves
Block replication will stop on DataNodes immediately
Clients can no longer read files even if NameNode is healthy
questions.shortExplanation: The NameNode is a Single Point of Failure — if it goes down, all of HDFS is unreachable.
questions.explanation: In classic Hadoop, the NameNode keeps the entire filesystem metadata, including directory tree, permissions, and the block-to-DataNode map, in its RAM on one machine. Clients must contact the NameNode for every file lookup, so if that one server crashes or its disk dies, the cluster cannot resolve any path even though the DataNodes still hold all the blocks. This makes the NameNode a Single Point of Failure (SPOF). Production clusters therefore add High Availability with a standby NameNode. The other options claim DataNodes lose data on reboot, that the cluster splits in two, that replication stops at the wrong moment, or that reads still work without the NameNode, all of which misunderstand how HDFS metadata works.

questions.text: A new engineer asks, "Why does Hadoop run a Secondary NameNode if it doesn't take over on failure?" Which answer correctly describes the Secondary NameNode's actual role?
options: It is a hot standby that automatically takes over when the primary fails
It executes MapReduce jobs in parallel with the primary
It performs housekeeping — merging fsimage and edits log — and helps rebuild a failed NameNode but is not a hot standby
It stores actual data blocks of HDFS
It assigns Mapper and Reducer tasks to DataNodes
questions.shortExplanation: The Secondary NameNode does housekeeping by merging fsimage and edits log; it is NOT a hot standby.
questions.explanation: Many beginners think the Secondary NameNode automatically takes over when the primary fails, but that is wrong. Its real job is to periodically read the primary's edit log and merge it with the fsimage to create a fresh checkpoint. This keeps the primary's startup time short and gives operators a recent snapshot to use if the primary needs to be rebuilt. It does not run user jobs, does not store blocks, and does not perform automatic failover. True hot standby is provided by the HA NameNode setup, not by the Secondary NameNode. The other options falsely call it a hot standby, claim it executes MapReduce, say it stores HDFS blocks, or that it schedules tasks, none of which match its actual housekeeping role.

questions.text: A 3-rack Hadoop cluster stores a file with replication factor 3. The administrator is configuring rack awareness. According to standard HDFS rack-awareness policy taught in the course, where will the three replicas be placed?
options: All three replicas on the same node
One replica each on three different racks (one per rack)
First replica on Rack 1, and the second and third replicas on Rack 2
All three replicas on Rack 3 only
Two replicas on the client node and one on a random rack
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS places the first replica on Rack 1 and the second and third on a different Rack 2.
questions.explanation: Hadoop's rack-awareness policy balances reliability with network cost. The first replica is written on the local node, which is on the client's rack (Rack 1). The second and third replicas are then placed on two different nodes inside a single different rack (Rack 2). This way, losing any one rack still leaves a usable replica, and the replication traffic does not have to cross three different racks. It is faster than putting one replica on every rack while still surviving a full rack failure. The other options either pile all replicas on one node or rack, spread them across three racks, or place them oddly on the client and a random rack, none of which match Hadoop's documented rack-aware placement.

questions.text: A data engineer uploads a 250 MB file into HDFS with default block size 128 MB. How many blocks will HDFS create for this file?
options: 1 block of 250 MB
2 blocks: one 128 MB and one 122 MB
3 blocks of equal size 128 MB each
250 blocks of 1 MB each
The upload will fail because file size exceeds block size
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS splits the file into 128 MB blocks plus one smaller block for the remaining bytes.
questions.explanation: HDFS stores files by chopping them into fixed-size blocks, with 128 MB as the default. If a file does not divide evenly, the last block is simply smaller and is not padded out. So a file is divided into as many full 128 MB blocks as fit, plus one final block that holds whatever is left. This avoids wasting space and keeps reads efficient, since only the actual bytes are stored on disk and replicated across DataNodes. The other options either pretend the whole file is one block, force every block to be exactly 128 MB with padding, split it into tiny 1 MB pieces, or claim the upload fails, none of which match how HDFS handles block sizing.

questions.text: The architecture team is studying the CAP theorem. A senior engineer claims, "A distributed system can only guarantee 2 of the 3 CAP properties simultaneously." What do C, A, and P stand for in this context?
options: Caching, Atomicity, Persistence
Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance
Concurrency, Asynchronicity, Performance
Containers, Auto-scaling, Pods
Commit, Abort, Persist
questions.shortExplanation: CAP stands for Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance.
questions.explanation: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a distributed datastore cannot guarantee all three of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance at the same time, so the designer must pick two. Consistency means every read sees the latest committed write. Availability means every request gets a response. Partition Tolerance means the system keeps working even when network links between nodes break. Most modern distributed databases trade some Consistency for Availability under partition. The other options list caching, atomicity, concurrency, containers, or commit/abort terms which come from different fields like transactions, Kubernetes, or hardware caches and have nothing to do with the CAP theorem.

questions.text: A Hadoop architect explains that HDFS is designed for "Write Once Read Many" (WORM). A junior engineer wants to know which workload is therefore a POOR fit for HDFS. Which is it?
options: Batch analytics on historical web logs
A high-frequency OLTP application with constant row-level updates
Storing terabytes of immutable sensor archives
Large-scale ETL processing of CSVs
Read-heavy analytical queries over petabytes
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS is Write-Once-Read-Many, so a high-frequency OLTP update workload is a poor fit.
questions.explanation: HDFS is built to write large files once and then read them many times for analytics. It does not support efficient random updates or row-level edits because every change would mean rewriting big blocks across multiple replicas. An OLTP system, like a banking or order-entry application, constantly performs small inserts and updates per second, which is exactly the pattern HDFS handles badly. For such workloads a relational or NoSQL OLTP database is the correct choice, not HDFS. Batch analytics, immutable archives, ETL rewrites of whole partitions, and large read-heavy analytical queries are all read-many or append-only patterns that HDFS handles well, so they are not poor fits.

questions.text: A junior developer is reviewing the four properties of an ACID transaction in MongoDB. They want to know which property guarantees that "either ALL operations of a transaction succeed, or NONE are applied — preventing partial updates." Which property is being described?
options: Consistency
Isolation
Atomicity
Durability
Availability
questions.shortExplanation: Atomicity means all operations in a transaction succeed together, or none of them are applied.
questions.explanation: Atomicity is the ACID property that treats a transaction as one indivisible unit. Either every step inside the transaction commits successfully, or if anything fails the database rolls back everything as if it never happened. This stops partial updates such as money being debited from one account without being credited to the other. In MongoDB multi-document transactions, this guarantee is enforced by the commit and abort protocol so the data never ends up in a half-updated state. Consistency enforces constraints, Isolation hides concurrent changes, Durability is about surviving crashes, and Availability is not an ACID property at all, so none of them describe the all-or-nothing rule.

questions.text: A team is told that in an ACID transaction, after a commit, the data must "survive crashes, restarts, and power failures." Which ACID property guarantees this?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
Partition Tolerance
questions.shortExplanation: Durability means committed data survives crashes, restarts, and power failures.
questions.explanation: Once a transaction is committed, Durability promises that its results are written to permanent storage and will not disappear, even if the server crashes, the kernel panics, or the power is suddenly cut. Databases achieve this by flushing the write-ahead log or journal to disk before reporting success. After recovery, the system replays this log to restore committed changes. Without Durability, users could see their save succeed and then lose it on the next restart, which is unacceptable for systems like banking or healthcare. Atomicity is about all-or-nothing within a transaction, Consistency is about valid states, Isolation is about concurrent access, and Partition Tolerance is a CAP property not an ACID one, so they do not cover crash survival.

questions.text: A bank's grade-update service rejects an update because it tried to set a grade to "Z" instead of an allowed value (A, B, C, D, F), and aborts the transaction. Which ACID property is being enforced?
options: Atomicity
Consistency — DB moves from one valid state to another, enforcing all rules and constraints
Isolation
Durability
Partition Tolerance
questions.shortExplanation: Consistency means the database moves from one valid state to another, respecting all rules.
questions.explanation: The Consistency property guarantees that every committed transaction leaves the database in a valid state where all constraints, types, and business rules still hold. If a transaction tries to break a rule, such as setting a field to a value outside the allowed list, the whole transaction is rejected and rolled back. This way the database can never silently store invalid data. Consistency is enforced by checks like data types, foreign keys, unique constraints, and custom validation rules defined in the schema. Atomicity is about indivisibility, Isolation is about concurrent reads, Durability is about crash survival, and Partition Tolerance belongs to CAP, so none of them describe schema or constraint enforcement.

questions.text: Two concurrent banking sessions read the same account during a transfer. The system guarantees that each session sees either the OLD balance or the FINAL balance, but never an intermediate (partially-updated) value. Which ACID property is this?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
Persistence
questions.shortExplanation: Isolation hides intermediate states so each transaction sees only fully old or fully new values.
questions.explanation: Isolation makes concurrent transactions appear as if they ran one after the other. While one transaction is updating a row, other transactions see either the original value or the final committed value, never a half-applied intermediate state. This prevents bugs like dirty reads where a balance briefly looks wrong during a transfer. The database enforces Isolation through locks, snapshots, or multi-version concurrency control depending on the isolation level chosen. Atomicity is about all-or-nothing per transaction, Consistency is about constraints, Durability is about surviving crashes, and Persistence is not a formal ACID term, so they do not describe protection against intermediate reads.

questions.text: A startup hears about the "4 V's of Big Data" — Volume, Variety, Velocity, Veracity. Their data is mostly TB-scale, mixed structured/unstructured, generated per-second from social streams, but also full of noise and inconsistencies from crowd-sourced reviews. Which of the 4 V's is BEST captured by the "noise and inconsistencies" alone?
options: Volume
Variety
Velocity
Veracity
Visualization
questions.shortExplanation: Veracity is the V about trust — noise, spam, bots, sarcasm, and inconsistencies in data.
questions.explanation: Among the 4Vs of Big Data, Veracity is the one that captures how trustworthy and clean the data is. Crowd-sourced reviews, social media posts, and sensor feeds often contain spam, bots, sarcasm, mis-spellings, and contradictory entries. Volume, Velocity, and Variety describe how much, how fast, and how mixed the data is, but they do not say anything about correctness. Veracity directly addresses that uncertainty, and pipelines must use cleaning, deduplication, and validation to handle it. Volume is about size, Variety is about format mix, Velocity is about speed, and Visualization is about presentation, so none of them describe the trust and noise problem the question highlights.

questions.text: A team is designing a system where producers send messages to "topics" that are split into partitions for horizontal scalability. Consumers join "consumer groups" so each message is processed once across the group. ZooKeeper coordinates the brokers. Which distributed technology matches this architecture?
options: Redis
Apache Kafka
Kubernetes
RabbitMQ
MongoDB ACID
questions.shortExplanation: Apache Kafka uses topics, partitions, consumer groups, and ZooKeeper for coordination.
questions.explanation: Kafka is a distributed streaming platform where producers publish to named topics. Each topic is split into partitions so messages can be spread across brokers for horizontal scaling. Consumers join a consumer group, and Kafka makes sure each message is processed by only one consumer inside that group. ZooKeeper (or KRaft in newer versions) coordinates broker metadata, partition leaders, and failover. This design supports very high throughput and replay of past messages. Redis is a cache, Kubernetes is a container orchestrator, RabbitMQ uses exchanges and queues without partitioned topic logs, and MongoDB ACID is a database not a message bus, so none of them match this architecture.

questions.text: A client wants to write a file to HDFS. The NameNode returns a pipeline of DataNodes [DN1, DN2, DN3] for replication. How does the client write the data to achieve replication factor 3?
options: The client writes the entire file three separate times to each DataNode
The client writes to DN1, which forwards the block to DN2, which forwards to DN3, forming a replication pipeline
The Secondary NameNode performs the replication after the write completes
The NameNode itself stores all three replicas
Replication is not performed during write; it only happens on read
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS writes replicas as a pipeline: client → DN1 → DN2 → DN3.
questions.explanation: When a client writes a block, the NameNode hands back a pipeline of DataNodes for that block, such as DN1, DN2, DN3. The client streams the data to DN1, DN1 forwards it to DN2, and DN2 forwards it to DN3. The data moves through the pipeline in one direction while acknowledgments flow back the other way. The client does not have to upload the same block three times, network usage is reduced, and replication happens during the write itself instead of as a separate step. Writing the file three separate times wastes bandwidth, the Secondary NameNode never handles replication, the NameNode itself never stores blocks, and replication never happens only on read, so those options are all wrong.

questions.text: A platform engineer describes a system as an "open-source container orchestration platform" that automatically deploys, scales, and self-heals containerized applications across worker nodes coordinated by a control plane (API Server, Scheduler, etcd, Controller Manager). Which technology is being described?
options: Apache Kafka
RabbitMQ
Kubernetes (K8s)
Redis Cluster
Apache Hadoop YARN
questions.shortExplanation: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestrator with a control plane and worker nodes.
questions.explanation: Kubernetes, often shortened to K8s, automates the deployment, scaling, and self-healing of containerized applications. The control plane is made of components like the API Server, Scheduler, etcd (cluster state store), and Controller Manager. Worker Nodes run the actual containers grouped inside Pods, and each node runs the kubelet and kube-proxy. When a Pod fails, the system automatically schedules a new one to keep the desired state. Kafka and RabbitMQ are messaging systems, Redis Cluster is an in-memory data store, and YARN only schedules Hadoop jobs, so none of them describe a full container orchestration platform with Pods and a control plane.

questions.text: A solutions architect describes Hadoop's strength as "moving computation to the data rather than data to the computation." What is the practical implication of this design philosophy?
options: Data must be streamed across the network for every job, increasing bandwidth use
Map tasks are scheduled on the DataNodes that already hold the relevant blocks, reducing network traffic and increasing speed
Computation is always centralized on the NameNode
The cluster cannot scale beyond a single rack
Data must be copied to a separate compute cluster before processing
questions.shortExplanation: Hadoop moves computation to the data, so Map tasks run where the blocks already live.
questions.explanation: Instead of pulling huge amounts of data across the network to a central computer, Hadoop sends the small Map task code to whichever DataNode already holds the required block. This idea is called data locality. It saves a huge amount of network bandwidth because the computation happens beside the disk, and the cluster scales smoothly because the work spreads out wherever the data was originally placed. Only the much smaller intermediate results need to move during the shuffle phase. Massive network shuffles, centralized NameNode computation, single-rack limits, and copying to a separate compute cluster all describe the opposite of data locality and would make the system slow and unscalable.

One replica each on three different racks
First replica on Rack 1, with the second and third replicas on Rack 2
All three replicas on the same rack as the client
Two replicas on the client's local node and one on a random rack

questions.explanation: Hadoop's rack-awareness policy balances reliability with network cost. The first replica is written on the local node, which is on the client's rack (Rack 1). The second and third replicas are then placed on two different nodes inside a single different rack (Rack 2). This way, losing any one rack still leaves a usable replica, and the replication traffic does not have to cross three different racks. It is faster than putting one replica on every rack while still surviving a full rack failure. questions.text: A data engineer copies a 300 MB file into HDFS using the default block size of 128 MB. How many physical blocks will HDFS allocate for it?
options: 1 block of 300 MB
3 blocks: two of 128 MB and one of 44 MB
3 blocks of exactly 128 MB each (rest is padded)
300 blocks of 1 MB each
The write fails because the file exceeds the default block size
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS splits the file into 128 MB blocks plus one smaller block for the remaining bytes.
questions.explanation: HDFS stores files by chopping them into fixed-size blocks, with 128 MB as the default. If a file does not divide evenly, the last block is simply smaller and is not padded out. So a file is divided into as many full 128 MB blocks as fit, plus one final block that holds whatever is left. This avoids wasting space and keeps reads efficient, since only the actual bytes are stored on disk and replicated across DataNodes. The other options either pretend the whole file is one block, force every block to be exactly 128 MB with padding, split it into tiny 1 MB pieces, or claim the upload fails, none of which match how HDFS handles block sizing.

questions.text: A systems-design candidate is asked about the CAP theorem during an interview. The interviewer states: "Under a network partition, a distributed datastore can guarantee at most TWO of the three CAP properties simultaneously." What do C, A, and P stand for?
options: Caching, Atomicity, Persistence
Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance
Concurrency, Atomic-broadcast, Performance
Containers, Auto-scaling, Pods
Commit, Abort, Persist
questions.shortExplanation: CAP stands for Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance.
questions.explanation: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a distributed datastore cannot guarantee all three of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance at the same time, so the designer must pick two. Consistency means every read sees the latest committed write. Availability means every request gets a response. Partition Tolerance means the system keeps working even when network links between nodes break. Most modern distributed databases trade some Consistency for Availability under partition. The other options list caching, atomicity, concurrency, containers, or commit/abort terms which come from different fields like transactions, Kubernetes, or hardware caches and have nothing to do with the CAP theorem.

questions.text: A Hadoop instructor describes HDFS as "Write Once, Read Many" (WORM). Based on this design, which workload would be a POOR fit for HDFS storage?
options: Batch analytics over years of historical clickstream logs
An OLTP banking application with thousands of row-level updates per second
An immutable archive of seismic sensor readings
ETL pipelines that periodically rewrite entire CSV partitions
Petabyte-scale read-heavy analytical queries
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS is Write-Once-Read-Many, so a high-frequency OLTP update workload is a poor fit.
questions.explanation: HDFS is built to write large files once and then read them many times for analytics. It does not support efficient random updates or row-level edits because every change would mean rewriting big blocks across multiple replicas. An OLTP system, like a banking or order-entry application, constantly performs small inserts and updates per second, which is exactly the pattern HDFS handles badly. For such workloads a relational or NoSQL OLTP database is the correct choice, not HDFS. Batch analytics, immutable archives, ETL rewrites of whole partitions, and large read-heavy analytical queries are all read-many or append-only patterns that HDFS handles well, so they are not poor fits.

questions.text: A junior developer reviews MongoDB ACID transactions. The instructor poses: "Which property ensures that ALL the operations in a transaction succeed together, or NONE of them are applied — preventing partial updates such as a debit without the corresponding credit?"
options: Consistency
Isolation
Atomicity
Durability
Availability
questions.shortExplanation: Atomicity means all operations in a transaction succeed together, or none of them are applied.
questions.explanation: Atomicity is the ACID property that treats a transaction as one indivisible unit. Either every step inside the transaction commits successfully, or if anything fails the database rolls back everything as if it never happened. This stops partial updates such as money being debited from one account without being credited to the other. In MongoDB multi-document transactions, this guarantee is enforced by the commit and abort protocol so the data never ends up in a half-updated state. Consistency enforces constraints, Isolation hides concurrent changes, Durability is about surviving crashes, and Availability is not an ACID property at all, so none of them describe the all-or-nothing rule.

questions.text: A trainee is told: "After a transaction commits in MongoDB, the changes must survive a sudden hardware power-off or kernel crash." Which ACID property guarantees this behavior?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
Partition Tolerance
questions.shortExplanation: Durability means committed data survives crashes, restarts, and power failures.
questions.explanation: Once a transaction is committed, Durability promises that its results are written to permanent storage and will not disappear, even if the server crashes, the kernel panics, or the power is suddenly cut. Databases achieve this by flushing the write-ahead log or journal to disk before reporting success. After recovery, the system replays this log to restore committed changes. Without Durability, users could see their save succeed and then lose it on the next restart, which is unacceptable for systems like banking or healthcare. Atomicity is about all-or-nothing within a transaction, Consistency is about valid states, Isolation is about concurrent access, and Partition Tolerance is a CAP property not an ACID one, so they do not cover crash survival.

questions.text: A university gradebook service tries to update a course grade to the value "Q". The system rejects the change and rolls back the transaction because only A, B, C, D, F are allowed by the schema rule. Which ACID property is being enforced?
options: Atomicity
Consistency — the database must move from one valid state to another, respecting all rules and constraints
Isolation
Durability
Partition Tolerance
questions.shortExplanation: Consistency means the database moves from one valid state to another, respecting all rules.
questions.explanation: The Consistency property guarantees that every committed transaction leaves the database in a valid state where all constraints, types, and business rules still hold. If a transaction tries to break a rule, such as setting a field to a value outside the allowed list, the whole transaction is rejected and rolled back. This way the database can never silently store invalid data. Consistency is enforced by checks like data types, foreign keys, unique constraints, and custom validation rules defined in the schema. Atomicity is about indivisibility, Isolation is about concurrent reads, Durability is about crash survival, and Partition Tolerance belongs to CAP, so none of them describe schema or constraint enforcement.

questions.text: Two ATM withdrawals on the same account run at the same time. The bank guarantees that each transaction sees either the pre-withdrawal balance or the post-withdrawal balance, never an intermediate, partially-updated balance. Which ACID property describes this guarantee?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
Persistence
questions.shortExplanation: Isolation hides intermediate states so each transaction sees only fully old or fully new values.
questions.explanation: Isolation makes concurrent transactions appear as if they ran one after the other. While one transaction is updating a row, other transactions see either the original value or the final committed value, never a half-applied intermediate state. This prevents bugs like dirty reads where a balance briefly looks wrong during a transfer. The database enforces Isolation through locks, snapshots, or multi-version concurrency control depending on the isolation level chosen. Atomicity is about all-or-nothing per transaction, Consistency is about constraints, Durability is about surviving crashes, and Persistence is not a formal ACID term, so they do not describe protection against intermediate reads.

questions.text: A startup ingests crowd-sourced product reviews where many entries contain spam, mis-spellings, sarcasm, and contradictory ratings. Reviews are at TB-scale, mixed format, and arrive every second. Among the 4 V's of Big Data, which V is BEST captured by the "spam, mis-spellings, sarcasm, and contradictions" alone?
options: Volume
Variety
Velocity
Veracity
Visualization
questions.shortExplanation: Veracity is the V about trust — noise, spam, bots, sarcasm, and inconsistencies in data.
questions.explanation: Among the 4Vs of Big Data, Veracity is the one that captures how trustworthy and clean the data is. Crowd-sourced reviews, social media posts, and sensor feeds often contain spam, bots, sarcasm, mis-spellings, and contradictory entries. Volume, Velocity, and Variety describe how much, how fast, and how mixed the data is, but they do not say anything about correctness. Veracity directly addresses that uncertainty, and pipelines must use cleaning, deduplication, and validation to handle it. Volume is about size, Variety is about format mix, Velocity is about speed, and Visualization is about presentation, so none of them describe the trust and noise problem the question highlights.

questions.text: An architect is designing a system where producers publish messages to "topics", topics are split into partitions for horizontal scalability, consumers are organized in groups so each message is processed once across a group, and ZooKeeper handles broker coordination and leader election. Which distributed technology matches?
options: Redis
Apache Kafka
Kubernetes
RabbitMQ
MongoDB ACID
questions.shortExplanation: Apache Kafka uses topics, partitions, consumer groups, and ZooKeeper for coordination.
questions.explanation: Kafka is a distributed streaming platform where producers publish to named topics. Each topic is split into partitions so messages can be spread across brokers for horizontal scaling. Consumers join a consumer group, and Kafka makes sure each message is processed by only one consumer inside that group. ZooKeeper (or KRaft in newer versions) coordinates broker metadata, partition leaders, and failover. This design supports very high throughput and replay of past messages. Redis is a cache, Kubernetes is a container orchestrator, RabbitMQ uses exchanges and queues without partitioned topic logs, and MongoDB ACID is a database not a message bus, so none of them match this architecture.

questions.text: An HDFS client wants to write a file with replication factor 3. The NameNode returns a pipeline of DataNodes [DN1, DN2, DN3]. How is the data physically replicated during the write?
options: The client uploads the entire file to each of the 3 DataNodes separately
The client writes to DN1; DN1 forwards the block to DN2; DN2 forwards it to DN3 — a replication pipeline
The Secondary NameNode replicates the file after the client write completes
The NameNode itself stores all 3 replicas in its RAM
Replication occurs only on the first read, not during write
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS writes replicas as a pipeline: client → DN1 → DN2 → DN3.
questions.explanation: When a client writes a block, the NameNode hands back a pipeline of DataNodes for that block, such as DN1, DN2, DN3. The client streams the data to DN1, DN1 forwards it to DN2, and DN2 forwards it to DN3. The data moves through the pipeline in one direction while acknowledgments flow back the other way. The client does not have to upload the same block three times, network usage is reduced, and replication happens during the write itself instead of as a separate step. Writing the file three separate times wastes bandwidth, the Secondary NameNode never handles replication, the NameNode itself never stores blocks, and replication never happens only on read, so those options are all wrong.

questions.text: A DevOps lead describes a platform that automates deployment, scaling, and self-healing of containerized apps, has a Control Plane (API Server, Scheduler, etcd, Controller Manager) and Worker Nodes running Pods. Which platform is being described?
options: Apache Kafka
RabbitMQ
Kubernetes (K8s)
Redis Cluster
Apache Hadoop YARN
questions.shortExplanation: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestrator with a control plane and worker nodes.
questions.explanation: Kubernetes, often shortened to K8s, automates the deployment, scaling, and self-healing of containerized applications. The control plane is made of components like the API Server, Scheduler, etcd (cluster state store), and Controller Manager. Worker Nodes run the actual containers grouped inside Pods, and each node runs the kubelet and kube-proxy. When a Pod fails, the system automatically schedules a new one to keep the desired state. Kafka and RabbitMQ are messaging systems, Redis Cluster is an in-memory data store, and YARN only schedules Hadoop jobs, so none of them describe a full container orchestration platform with Pods and a control plane.

questions.text: A Hadoop instructor states that the framework's key idea is to "move code to the data rather than data to the code". What is the practical operational implication?
options: Massive data shuffles across the network on every job, increasing bandwidth usage
Map tasks are scheduled on the DataNodes that already hold the relevant blocks (data locality), reducing network I/O
Computation is always centralized on the NameNode
The framework cannot scale beyond a single rack
All data must first be copied to a separate compute cluster
questions.shortExplanation: Hadoop moves computation to the data, so Map tasks run where the blocks already live.
questions.explanation: Instead of pulling huge amounts of data across the network to a central computer, Hadoop sends the small Map task code to whichever DataNode already holds the required block. This idea is called data locality. It saves a huge amount of network bandwidth because the computation happens beside the disk, and the cluster scales smoothly because the work spreads out wherever the data was originally placed. Only the much smaller intermediate results need to move during the shuffle phase. Massive network shuffles, centralized NameNode computation, single-rack limits, and copying to a separate compute cluster all describe the opposite of data locality and would make the system slow and unscalable.

questions.text: A weather-forecasting agency processes satellite imagery (multi-petabyte), live storm sensor feeds arriving every few hundred milliseconds, and unstructured field observation reports. The team lead labels this a "Big Data" workload. Which combination BEST justifies that label?
options: Small daily extracts stored in a single Postgres instance with a strict schema
Predictable batch loads with centralized control over a single database
PB-scale Volume, sub-second Velocity, and mixed structured + unstructured Variety
Purely structured records with low frequency
Strict OLTP semantics with row-level updates required
questions.shortExplanation: Big Data is justified by huge Volume, fast Velocity, and mixed Variety together.
questions.explanation: A workload qualifies as Big Data when it shows three things at once: enormous size measured in terabytes or petabytes, very fast arrival speed such as per-second or millisecond streams, and a mix of data formats including structured tables, semi-structured logs, and unstructured text or media. A single traditional database server cannot keep up with all three at the same time, so a distributed platform is needed. These three together are commonly called the 3Vs of Big Data. The case described in the question shows all three signals, which is why the architect labels it a Big Data problem. The other options describe small, predictable, centrally managed, single-schema, or purely transactional systems, which are the opposite of a Big Data workload and do not need a distributed Big Data platform.

questions.text: A government tax department runs a centralized RDBMS handling Gigabytes of structured returns with a strict schema. The new CIO is migrating to a Big Data platform for fraud-pattern analytics. What is the MOST important architectural difference to plan for?
options: Both platforms require the same single high-end machine
The Big Data platform uses distributed storage and a flexible/dynamic schema rather than centralized strict-schema management
Big Data systems handle only structured records and outperform RDBMS for OLTP
The RDBMS data is inherently harder to manage than Big Data
Both yield identical data velocity and integration patterns
questions.shortExplanation: Big Data uses distributed storage with a flexible schema instead of one strict central RDBMS.
questions.explanation: Traditional RDBMS systems keep all data on a single powerful server and force every record into a fixed schema set in advance. A Big Data platform like Hadoop spreads data across many low-cost machines and accepts data in flexible or dynamic formats, including JSON, logs, and images. This shift removes the single-server limit and lets the team grow storage and compute by adding more nodes. It also means planning for distributed file layouts, replication, and tools like Hive or Spark rather than pure SQL. The other options wrongly claim both systems need the same hardware, that Big Data only handles structured data, that RDBMS is harder to manage, or that velocities and patterns match, none of which reflect the real architectural shift.

questions.text: A real-time gaming startup's data volume jumps from 8 TB/year to 8 PB/year. The Ops Manager argues for buying one massive server with extreme RAM/CPU. The Data Engineer argues for a 120-node commodity cluster. Identify the scaling strategies represented.
options: Both are horizontal scaling
Ops Manager → horizontal; Data Engineer → vertical
Ops Manager → vertical scaling; Data Engineer → horizontal scaling
Both are vertical scaling
Neither is a recognized scaling strategy
questions.shortExplanation: Vertical scaling means a bigger single machine; horizontal scaling means more machines.
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling, also called scaling up, upgrades a single server with more RAM, more CPU, or faster disks. Horizontal scaling, also called scaling out, adds more commodity machines into a cluster and shares the work across them. Vertical scaling is simple but hits a hardware ceiling and costs a lot at the top end. Horizontal scaling is the Big Data approach because it grows almost linearly with petabyte-scale data and tolerates node failures. The wrong options swap the two strategies, claim both teams use the same one, or deny that either is a real scaling strategy, all of which contradict the standard definitions taught in distributed computing.

questions.text: A fintech firm runs a 2,000-node cluster for fraud detection. A new analyst asks what makes this cluster qualify as a "distributed system" instead of a giant parallel computer. Which justification is MOST accurate?
options: All 2,000 nodes share one physical memory bus and CPU socket
Nodes are interconnected over a network, present themselves as a single logical service to clients, and a single node failure does not crash the whole service
Only one node performs computation; the others sit idle
The whole cluster halts the instant any one node fails
There is no real distinction — "distributed" and "parallel" are synonyms
questions.shortExplanation: A distributed system is many networked nodes that look like one service and survive node failures.
questions.explanation: A parallel computer is a single machine that uses many CPUs sharing the same memory and bus. A distributed system is many separate machines connected by a network. To the client they appear as one single logical service, but each node runs on its own. If one node crashes, the others keep serving requests, so the whole service does not go down. This network-based design is what makes Hadoop, Spark, and Kafka clusters truly distributed rather than just parallel. The other options confuse parallel and distributed, claim all nodes share one memory bus, say only one node computes, or wrongly state that one failure crashes the cluster, none of which match a real distributed architecture.

questions.text: A CTO summarizes the case for moving from a single-server RDBMS to a distributed computing platform. They cite three benefits to the board. Which set captures the MAIN benefits as taught?
options: Performance, Scalability, Fault Tolerance
Vendor lock-in, Strict schema, Single point of failure
Vertical scaling, Single node, Manual recovery
ACID guarantees, Synchronous replication, Centralization
Manual failover, Hardware redundancy only, Strict transactionality
questions.shortExplanation: The three main benefits are Performance, Scalability, and Fault Tolerance.
questions.explanation: Distributed computing wins on three points compared to a single server. Performance improves because tasks run in parallel on many nodes at once. Scalability improves because more machines can be added when data grows, without rewriting the system. Fault Tolerance improves because replication and failover let the cluster keep working even when individual nodes die. These three benefits together are the reason companies move from a single RDBMS to a Hadoop or Spark cluster. The other options list weaknesses such as vendor lock-in, single point of failure, vertical-only scaling, or manual failover, which are problems of centralized systems and not benefits of distributed ones.

questions.text: In a Hadoop cluster, the NameNode holds the entire filesystem hierarchy, ACLs, replication factor, and block map in RAM on a single machine. A reliability engineer is asked to name the most critical risk of this design. Which is it?
options: DataNodes will lose their stored blocks when the NameNode restarts
NameNode is a single point of failure — its failure renders the whole HDFS inaccessible
The cluster will split-brain into two competing namespaces
Block replication on DataNodes halts the moment the NameNode is healthy
Clients can still read files even if the NameNode is unreachable
questions.shortExplanation: The NameNode is a Single Point of Failure — if it goes down, all of HDFS is unreachable.
questions.explanation: In classic Hadoop, the NameNode keeps the entire filesystem metadata, including directory tree, permissions, and the block-to-DataNode map, in its RAM on one machine. Clients must contact the NameNode for every file lookup, so if that one server crashes or its disk dies, the cluster cannot resolve any path even though the DataNodes still hold all the blocks. This makes the NameNode a Single Point of Failure (SPOF). Production clusters therefore add High Availability with a standby NameNode. The other options claim DataNodes lose data on reboot, that the cluster splits in two, that replication stops at the wrong moment, or that reads still work without the NameNode, all of which misunderstand how HDFS metadata works.

questions.text: A trainee asks: "If the Secondary NameNode does NOT take over when the primary fails, then what does it actually do?" Which explanation is correct?
options: It is a hot standby that automatically takes over on failure
It runs user MapReduce jobs alongside the primary
It performs housekeeping by merging fsimage and edits log, and can help rebuild a failed NameNode — but it is NOT a hot standby
It physically stores HDFS data blocks
It schedules Mapper and Reducer slots on TaskTrackers
questions.shortExplanation: The Secondary NameNode does housekeeping by merging fsimage and edits log; it is NOT a hot standby.
questions.explanation: Many beginners think the Secondary NameNode automatically takes over when the primary fails, but that is wrong. Its real job is to periodically read the primary's edit log and merge it with the fsimage to create a fresh checkpoint. This keeps the primary's startup time short and gives operators a recent snapshot to use if the primary needs to be rebuilt. It does not run user jobs, does not store blocks, and does not perform automatic failover. True hot standby is provided by the HA NameNode setup, not by the Secondary NameNode. The other options falsely call it a hot standby, claim it executes MapReduce, say it stores HDFS blocks, or that it schedules tasks, none of which match its actual housekeeping role.

questions.text: An engineer is designing a system where producers publish to "topics", topics are partitioned for horizontal scalability, consumer groups read each message exactly once, and ZooKeeper coordinates broker metadata and leader election. Which technology matches?
options: Redis
Apache Kafka
Kubernetes
RabbitMQ
MongoDB ACID
questions.shortExplanation: Apache Kafka uses topics, partitions, consumer groups, and ZooKeeper for coordination.
questions.explanation: Kafka is a distributed streaming platform where producers publish to named topics. Each topic is split into partitions so messages can be spread across brokers for horizontal scaling. Consumers join a consumer group, and Kafka makes sure each message is processed by only one consumer inside that group. ZooKeeper (or KRaft in newer versions) coordinates broker metadata, partition leaders, and failover. This design supports very high throughput and replay of past messages. questions.text: An HDFS client must write a file with replication factor 3. The NameNode returns a pipeline [DN1, DN2, DN3]. How is data physically replicated during the write?
options: The client uploads the entire file 3 times to each DataNode separately
The client writes to DN1; DN1 forwards the block to DN2; DN2 forwards it to DN3 — a replication pipeline
The Secondary NameNode replicates the file after the client write completes
The NameNode stores all 3 replicas in RAM itself
Replication occurs only on the first read, not during write
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS writes replicas as a pipeline: client → DN1 → DN2 → DN3.
questions.explanation: When a client writes a block, the NameNode hands back a pipeline of DataNodes for that block, such as DN1, DN2, DN3. The client streams the data to DN1, DN1 forwards it to DN2, and DN2 forwards it to DN3. The data moves through the pipeline in one direction while acknowledgments flow back the other way. The client does not have to upload the same block three times, network usage is reduced, and replication happens during the write itself instead of as a separate step. Writing the file three separate times wastes bandwidth, the Secondary NameNode never handles replication, the NameNode itself never stores blocks, and replication never happens only on read, so those options are all wrong.

questions.text: A platform engineer describes an open-source container orchestration system that auto-deploys, scales, and self-heals containerized apps, runs a Control Plane (API Server, Scheduler, etcd, Controller Manager) and Worker Nodes hosting Pods. Which technology is being described?

RabbitMQ
Kubernetes (K8s)
Redis Cluster
Apache Hadoop YARN

questions.explanation: Kubernetes, often shortened to K8s, automates the deployment, scaling, and self-healing of containerized applications. questions.text: An instructor states that Hadoop's key idea is "move computation to data rather than data to computation". What is the practical operational implication?
options: Massive data shuffles across the network for every job, raising bandwidth use
Map tasks are scheduled on the DataNodes already holding the relevant blocks (data locality), cutting network I/O
Computation is always centralized on the NameNode
The cluster cannot scale beyond a single rack
All data must first be copied to a separate compute cluster
questions.shortExplanation: Hadoop moves computation to the data, so Map tasks run where the blocks already live.
questions.explanation: Instead of pulling huge amounts of data across the network to a central computer, Hadoop sends the small Map task code to whichever DataNode already holds the required block. This idea is called data locality. It saves a huge amount of network bandwidth because the computation happens beside the disk, and the cluster scales smoothly because the work spreads out wherever the data was originally placed. Only the much smaller intermediate results need to move during the shuffle phase. Massive network shuffles, centralized NameNode computation, single-rack limits, and copying to a separate compute cluster all describe the opposite of data locality and would make the system slow and unscalable.

questions.text: An autonomous-vehicle company collects LIDAR point clouds (petabytes), real-time CAN-bus telemetry (millisecond rate), and unstructured driver-event logs into a unified analytics platform. The Chief Data Officer calls this a "Big Data" workload. Which combination BEST justifies that label?

Predictable nightly batches with centralized control
PB-scale Volume, millisecond Velocity, mixed structured + unstructured Variety
Purely structured transactions with row-level updates
OLTP-only access patterns
questions.shortExplanation: Big Data is justified by huge Volume, fast Velocity, and mixed Variety together.

The case described in the question shows all three signals, which is why the architect labels it a Big Data problem. questions.text: A national insurance company runs its claims system on a centralized RDBMS handling Gigabytes of structured records per day with a strict schema. The CTO plans to migrate to a Hadoop-based analytics platform. What is the MOST important architectural difference to plan for?
options: Both platforms require the same high-end single machine
The Hadoop platform relies on distributed storage and a flexible/dynamic schema, replacing centralized strict-schema management
Hadoop handles only structured records and outperforms RDBMS for OLTP
The RDBMS data is inherently harder to manage than Big Data
Both produce identical data velocity and integration patterns
questions.shortExplanation: Big Data uses distributed storage with a flexible schema instead of one strict central RDBMS.
questions.explanation: Traditional RDBMS systems keep all data on a single powerful server and force every record into a fixed schema set in advance. A Big Data platform like Hadoop spreads data across many low-cost machines and accepts data in flexible or dynamic formats, including JSON, logs, and images. This shift removes the single-server limit and lets the team grow storage and compute by adding more nodes. It also means planning for distributed file layouts, replication, and tools like Hive or Spark rather than pure SQL. The other options wrongly claim both systems need the same hardware, that Big Data only handles structured data, that RDBMS is harder to manage, or that velocities and patterns match, none of which reflect the real architectural shift.

questions.text: A digital-ads platform's data jumps from 4 TB/year to 4 PB/year. The Ops Lead recommends one massive server with extreme RAM/CPU. The Data Lead recommends a 90-node commodity cluster. Identify the scaling strategies represented.
options: Both are horizontal scaling
Ops Lead → horizontal; Data Lead → vertical
Ops Lead → vertical scaling; Data Lead → horizontal scaling
Both are vertical scaling
Neither is a recognized scaling strategy
questions.shortExplanation: Vertical scaling means a bigger single machine; horizontal scaling means more machines.
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling, also called scaling up, upgrades a single server with more RAM, more CPU, or faster disks. Horizontal scaling, also called scaling out, adds more commodity machines into a cluster and shares the work across them. Vertical scaling is simple but hits a hardware ceiling and costs a lot at the top end. Horizontal scaling is the Big Data approach because it grows almost linearly with petabyte-scale data and tolerates node failures. The wrong options swap the two strategies, claim both teams use the same one, or deny that either is a real scaling strategy, all of which contradict the standard definitions taught in distributed computing.

questions.text: A search-engine company runs a 3,000-node cluster for index building. A new manager asks why this counts as a "distributed system" rather than a giant parallel computer. Which justification is MOST accurate?
options: All 3,000 nodes share a single physical memory bus and CPU socket
Nodes are interconnected over a network, present themselves as a single logical service to clients, and individual node failures do not bring down the whole service
Only one node actually computes; the rest sit idle
The whole cluster halts the instant any single node fails
"Distributed" and "parallel" are exactly synonymous
questions.shortExplanation: A distributed system is many networked nodes that look like one service and survive node failures.
questions.explanation: A parallel computer is a single machine that uses many CPUs sharing the same memory and bus. A distributed system is many separate machines connected by a network. To the client they appear as one single logical service, but each node runs on its own. If one node crashes, the others keep serving requests, so the whole service does not go down. This network-based design is what makes Hadoop, Spark, and Kafka clusters truly distributed rather than just parallel. The other options confuse parallel and distributed, claim all nodes share one memory bus, say only one node computes, or wrongly state that one failure crashes the cluster, none of which match a real distributed architecture.

questions.text: A CIO pitches the move from a single-server RDBMS to a distributed computing platform, listing three benefits to the board. Which set captures the MAIN benefits as taught?
options: Performance, Scalability, Fault Tolerance
Vendor lock-in, Strict schema, Single point of failure
Vertical scaling, Single node, Manual recovery
ACID guarantees, Synchronous replication, Centralization
Manual failover, Hardware redundancy only, Strict transactionality
questions.shortExplanation: The three main benefits are Performance, Scalability, and Fault Tolerance.
questions.explanation: Distributed computing wins on three points compared to a single server. Performance improves because tasks run in parallel on many nodes at once. Scalability improves because more machines can be added when data grows, without rewriting the system. Fault Tolerance improves because replication and failover let the cluster keep working even when individual nodes die. These three benefits together are the reason companies move from a single RDBMS to a Hadoop or Spark cluster. The other options list weaknesses such as vendor lock-in, single point of failure, vertical-only scaling, or manual failover, which are problems of centralized systems and not benefits of distributed ones.

questions.text: A Hadoop NameNode holds the entire filesystem hierarchy, ACLs, replication info, and block-map in RAM on a single machine. A site-reliability engineer is asked to name the most critical operational risk. Which is it?
options: DataNodes will lose their stored blocks whenever the NameNode restarts
NameNode is a single point of failure — its loss makes the entire HDFS inaccessible
The cluster automatically splits into two competing namespaces
Block replication on DataNodes halts the moment the NameNode is healthy
Clients can still read files even if the NameNode is unreachable
questions.shortExplanation: The NameNode is a Single Point of Failure — if it goes down, all of HDFS is unreachable.
questions.explanation: In classic Hadoop, the NameNode keeps the entire filesystem metadata, including directory tree, permissions, and the block-to-DataNode map, in its RAM on one machine. Clients must contact the NameNode for every file lookup, so if that one server crashes or its disk dies, the cluster cannot resolve any path even though the DataNodes still hold all the blocks. This makes the NameNode a Single Point of Failure (SPOF). Production clusters therefore add High Availability with a standby NameNode. The other options claim DataNodes lose data on reboot, that the cluster splits in two, that replication stops at the wrong moment, or that reads still work without the NameNode, all of which misunderstand how HDFS metadata works.

questions.text: A trainee asks: "If the Secondary NameNode does not take over on failure, then what does it actually do?" Which explanation is correct?
options: It is a hot standby that automatically takes over on failure
It executes user MapReduce jobs alongside the primary
It performs housekeeping — merging fsimage and edits log — and can help rebuild a failed NameNode, but is NOT a hot standby
It physically stores HDFS data blocks
It schedules Mapper and Reducer slots on TaskTrackers
questions.shortExplanation: The Secondary NameNode does housekeeping by merging fsimage and edits log; it is NOT a hot standby.
questions.explanation: Many beginners think the Secondary NameNode automatically takes over when the primary fails, but that is wrong. Its real job is to periodically read the primary's edit log and merge it with the fsimage to create a fresh checkpoint. This keeps the primary's startup time short and gives operators a recent snapshot to use if the primary needs to be rebuilt. It does not run user jobs, does not store blocks, and does not perform automatic failover. True hot standby is provided by the HA NameNode setup, not by the Secondary NameNode. The other options falsely call it a hot standby, claim it executes MapReduce, say it stores HDFS blocks, or that it schedules tasks, none of which match its actual housekeeping role.

questions.text: A 3-rack Hadoop cluster with replication factor 3 writes a new file. According to the standard rack-awareness policy taught, where will the three replicas be placed?
options: All three replicas on one node
One replica per rack across three different racks
First replica on Rack 1, with second and third replicas on Rack 2
All three replicas on the same rack
Two replicas on the client node and one on a random rack
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS places the first replica on Rack 1 and the second and third on a different Rack 2.
questions.explanation: Hadoop's rack-awareness policy balances reliability with network cost. The first replica is written on the local node, which is on the client's rack (Rack 1). The second and third replicas are then placed on two different nodes inside a single different rack (Rack 2). This way, losing any one rack still leaves a usable replica, and the replication traffic does not have to cross three different racks. It is faster than putting one replica on every rack while still surviving a full rack failure. The other options either pile all replicas on one node or rack, spread them across three racks, or place them oddly on the client and a random rack, none of which match Hadoop's documented rack-aware placement.

questions.text: A data engineer uploads a 500 MB file into HDFS with default block size 128 MB. How many physical blocks will HDFS allocate?
options: 1 block of 500 MB
4 blocks: three of 128 MB and one of 116 MB
4 blocks of exactly 128 MB each
500 blocks of 1 MB each
The upload fails because the file exceeds the default block size
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS splits the file into 128 MB blocks plus one smaller block for the remaining bytes.
questions.explanation: HDFS stores files by chopping them into fixed-size blocks, with 128 MB as the default. If a file does not divide evenly, the last block is simply smaller and is not padded out. So a file is divided into as many full 128 MB blocks as fit, plus one final block that holds whatever is left. This avoids wasting space and keeps reads efficient, since only the actual bytes are stored on disk and replicated across DataNodes. The other options either pretend the whole file is one block, force every block to be exactly 128 MB with padding, split it into tiny 1 MB pieces, or claim the upload fails, none of which match how HDFS handles block sizing.

questions.text: A systems-design interviewer states: "Under a network partition, a distributed datastore can guarantee at most two of the three CAP properties." What do C, A, and P stand for?
options: Caching, Atomicity, Persistence
Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance
Concurrency, Atomic-broadcast, Performance
Containers, Auto-scaling, Pods
Commit, Abort, Persist
questions.shortExplanation: CAP stands for Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance.
questions.explanation: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a distributed datastore cannot guarantee all three of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance at the same time, so the designer must pick two. Consistency means every read sees the latest committed write. Availability means every request gets a response. Partition Tolerance means the system keeps working even when network links between nodes break. Most modern distributed databases trade some Consistency for Availability under partition. The other options list caching, atomicity, concurrency, containers, or commit/abort terms which come from different fields like transactions, Kubernetes, or hardware caches and have nothing to do with the CAP theorem.

questions.text: A Hadoop instructor describes HDFS as "Write Once Read Many" (WORM). Which workload is therefore a POOR fit for HDFS storage?
options: Batch analytics on years of historical click logs
A high-volume OLTP order-entry system with thousands of row-level updates per second
An immutable archive of seismic sensor readings
ETL pipelines that periodically rewrite whole CSV partitions
Petabyte-scale read-heavy analytical queries
questions.shortExplanation: HDFS is Write-Once-Read-Many, so a high-frequency OLTP update workload is a poor fit.
questions.explanation: HDFS is built to write large files once and then read them many times for analytics. It does not support efficient random updates or row-level edits because every change would mean rewriting big blocks across multiple replicas. An OLTP system, like a banking or order-entry application, constantly performs small inserts and updates per second, which is exactly the pattern HDFS handles badly. For such workloads a relational or NoSQL OLTP database is the correct choice, not HDFS. Batch analytics, immutable archives, ETL rewrites of whole partitions, and large read-heavy analytical queries are all read-many or append-only patterns that HDFS handles well, so they are not poor fits.

questions.text: A junior developer is reviewing MongoDB ACID properties. Which property guarantees that ALL operations in a transaction either succeed together or none are applied — preventing partial updates like a debit without a credit?
options: Consistency
Isolation
Atomicity
Durability
Availability
questions.shortExplanation: Atomicity means all operations in a transaction succeed together, or none of them are applied.
questions.explanation: Atomicity is the ACID property that treats a transaction as one indivisible unit. Either every step inside the transaction commits successfully, or if anything fails the database rolls back everything as if it never happened. This stops partial updates such as money being debited from one account without being credited to the other. In MongoDB multi-document transactions, this guarantee is enforced by the commit and abort protocol so the data never ends up in a half-updated state. Consistency enforces constraints, Isolation hides concurrent changes, Durability is about surviving crashes, and Availability is not an ACID property at all, so none of them describe the all-or-nothing rule.

questions.text: A trainee is told: "Once a transaction commits in MongoDB, the changes must persist across crashes, kernel panics, and power failures." Which ACID property guarantees this?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
Partition Tolerance
questions.shortExplanation: Durability means committed data survives crashes, restarts, and power failures.
questions.explanation: Once a transaction is committed, Durability promises that its results are written to permanent storage and will not disappear, even if the server crashes, the kernel panics, or the power is suddenly cut. Databases achieve this by flushing the write-ahead log or journal to disk before reporting success. After recovery, the system replays this log to restore committed changes. Without Durability, users could see their save succeed and then lose it on the next restart, which is unacceptable for systems like banking or healthcare. Atomicity is about all-or-nothing within a transaction, Consistency is about valid states, Isolation is about concurrent access, and Partition Tolerance is a CAP property not an ACID one, so they do not cover crash survival.

questions.text: A loan-approval service rejects an attempt to set a credit rating to "Z" — only allowed values are AAA, AA, A, B, C, D — and the entire transaction is aborted. Which ACID property is being enforced?
options: Atomicity
Consistency — the database must move from one valid state to another, respecting all rules and constraints
Isolation
Durability
Partition Tolerance
questions.shortExplanation: Consistency means the database moves from one valid state to another, respecting all rules.
questions.explanation: The Consistency property guarantees that every committed transaction leaves the database in a valid state where all constraints, types, and business rules still hold. If a transaction tries to break a rule, such as setting a field to a value outside the allowed list, the whole transaction is rejected and rolled back. This way the database can never silently store invalid data. Consistency is enforced by checks like data types, foreign keys, unique constraints, and custom validation rules defined in the schema. Atomicity is about indivisibility, Isolation is about concurrent reads, Durability is about crash survival, and Partition Tolerance belongs to CAP, so none of them describe schema or constraint enforcement.

questions.text: Two ATM withdrawals run concurrently on the same account. The system guarantees that each transaction sees either the pre-withdrawal balance or the post-withdrawal balance — never an intermediate, partially-updated balance. Which ACID property describes this?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
Persistence
questions.shortExplanation: Isolation hides intermediate states so each transaction sees only fully old or fully new values.
questions.explanation: Isolation makes concurrent transactions appear as if they ran one after the other. While one transaction is updating a row, other transactions see either the original value or the final committed value, never a half-applied intermediate state. This prevents bugs like dirty reads where a balance briefly looks wrong during a transfer. The database enforces Isolation through locks, snapshots, or multi-version concurrency control depending on the isolation level chosen. Atomicity is about all-or-nothing per transaction, Consistency is about constraints, Durability is about surviving crashes, and Persistence is not a formal ACID term, so they do not describe protection against intermediate reads.

Atomicity

questions.text: A trainee is told: "Once a transaction commits in MongoDB, the changes must persist across crashes, kernel panics, and power failures." Which ACID property guarantees this?

Isolation

Variety
Velocity
Veracity
Visualization

Volume is about size, Variety is about format mix, Velocity is about speed, and Visualization is about presentation, so none of them describe the trust and noise problem the question highlights.

questions.text: An engineer is designing a system where producers publish to "topics", topics are partitioned for horizontal scalability, consumer groups read each message exactly once, and ZooKeeper coordinates broker metadata and leader election. Which technology matches?

Apache Kafka
Kubernetes
RabbitMQ
MongoDB ACID

questions.explanation: Kafka is a distributed streaming platform where producers publish to named topics. Consumers join a consumer group, and Kafka makes sure each message is processed by only one consumer inside that group. Writing the file three separate times wastes bandwidth, the Secondary NameNode never handles replication, the NameNode itself never stores blocks, and replication never happens only on read, so those options are all wrong.

questions.text: A platform engineer describes an open-source container orchestration platform that auto-deploys, scales, and self-heals containerized apps, with a Control Plane (API Server, Scheduler, etcd, Controller Manager) and Worker Nodes hosting Pods. Which platform is being described?

RabbitMQ
Kubernetes (K8s)
Redis Cluster
Apache Hadoop YARN

Computation is always centralized on the NameNode
The cluster cannot scale beyond a single rack
All data must first be copied to a separate compute cluster

Both are vertical scaling

Nodes are interconnected over a network, appear as a single logical service to clients, and individual node failures do not bring down the whole service
Only one node actually computes; the rest sit idle
The whole cluster halts the instant any one node fails
"Distributed" and "parallel" are exactly synonymous
questions.shortExplanation: A distributed system is many networked nodes that look like one service and survive node failures.

The cluster automatically splits into two competing namespaces
Block replication on DataNodes halts the moment the NameNode is healthy
Clients can still read files even if the NameNode is unreachable

The other options claim DataNodes lose data on reboot, that the cluster splits in two, that replication stops at the wrong moment, or that reads still work without the NameNode, all of which misunderstand how HDFS metadata works.

questions.text: A trainee asks: "If the Secondary NameNode does NOT take over on failure, what does it actually do?" Which explanation is correct?

It runs user MapReduce jobs alongside the primary

It physically stores HDFS data blocks
It schedules Mapper and Reducer slots on TaskTrackers

One replica per rack across three different racks
First replica on Rack 1, second and third replicas on Rack 2
All three replicas on the same rack
Two replicas on the client node and one on a random rack

800 blocks of 1 MB each

questions.text: A systems-design instructor states: "Under a network partition, a distributed datastore can guarantee at most two of the three CAP properties simultaneously." What do C, A, and P stand for?

Concurrency, Atomic-broadcast, Performance
Containers, Auto-scaling, Pods
Commit, Abort, Persist

options: Batch analytics over years of historical sensor logs

An immutable archive of seismic sensor readings
ETL pipelines that periodically rewrite whole partitions
Petabyte-scale read-heavy analytical queries

Massive network shuffles, centralized NameNode computation, single-rack limits, and copying to a separate compute cluster all describe the opposite of data locality and would make the system slow and unscalable.
